## Building the cost from the ground up

**Step 1 — size the salt inventory.**
Solar salt (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃) has cp ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K ≈ 4.2×10⁻⁴ kWh/kg·K. Operated over the standard CSP range (~290°C cold tank → ~565°C hot tank, ΔT≈270K), each kg stores ≈0.11 kWh. For 5,000 kWh of thermal capacity:

mass ≈ 5,000 / 0.11 ≈ **45 tonnes of salt**

**Step 2 — price each subsystem (two-tank, pumped, electrically-chargeable design):**

| Component | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt (45 t @ ~$700–800/t) | commodity nitrate salt | ~$35k |
| Hot + cold tanks, insulated/lined, foundation heat-tracing | ~30 m³ each, high-temp alloy/refractory | ~$500k |
| Molten-salt pumps (hot + cold, long-shaft cantilever type) | specialty, low volume | ~$160k |
| Piping, valves, freeze-protection trace heating | corrosion- and temp-rated | ~$150k |
| Charge heaters + discharge heat exchanger | sized to ~0.8–1 MW charge/discharge rate | ~$200k |
| Instrumentation & controls | | ~$75k |
| Civil/structural/electrical | | ~$150k |
| **Direct equipment subtotal** | | **~$1.27M** |
| Installation labor (~25%) | | ~$320k |
| EPC, engineering, contingency (~25%) | | ~$400k |
| **Total installed cost** | | **~$2.0M** |

**→ ≈ $400/kWh of thermal storage capacity** (plausible range $250–600/kWh given tank/pump cost uncertainty).

Sanity check: utility-scale CSP molten-salt TES (hundreds of MWh) runs ~$20–30/kWh-th — roughly 15× cheaper per kWh than this estimate. That gap is real and expected: pumps, heat exchangers, controls, and labor are largely fixed costs that don't shrink with tank size, so a 5 MWh system pays almost the same "BOP tax" as a system 100× larger. Tanks and salt scale with volume; pumps, valves, heaters and controls don't.

## From storage capacity to delivered energy

Two things matter that a flat $/kWh figure hides: **round-trip efficiency** and **cycle life**.

- If used purely as *heat* storage (process heat, no reconversion to electricity), round-trip efficiency is ~95%+ — just insulation losses.
- If used as an **electricity storage "Carnot battery"** (charge via resistive heater, discharge via a steam/ORC turbine back to grid power) — the only basis comparable to lithium-ion — round-trip efficiency is much lower, typically **35–45%**, limited by the heat-engine discharge step. I'll use 40%.
- Cycle life: the salt itself doesn't chemically degrade with cycling (unlike Li-ion electrodes), so life is set by mechanical wear of pumps/valves and the 25–30 year plant design life. At ~1 cycle/day, that's **~10,000 cycles**.

Lifetime electrical energy delivered:
5,000 kWh × 0.40 RTE × 10,000 cycles ≈ **20 GWh delivered**

Capital cost per kWh delivered ≈ $2.0M / 20,000,000 kWh ≈ **$0.10/kWh** (capital only, excludes O&M and the extra charging electricity lost to the 60% conversion loss).

## Lithium-ion comparison (same 5 MWh, same method)

| | Molten salt (Carnot battery) | Li-ion |
|---|---|---|
| Installed cost | ~$400/kWh → $2.0M | ~$280/kWh → $1.4M |
| Round-trip efficiency | ~40% | ~88% |
| Cycle life | ~10,000 cycles (30 yr) | ~5,000 cycles (~15 yr, calendar-limited) |
| Lifetime energy delivered | ~20 GWh | ~25 GWh |
| **$/kWh delivered (capital only)** | **~$0.10** | **~$0.056** |

**At this scale and duration, lithium-ion wins** — roughly 1.8× cheaper per kWh delivered — despite molten salt's much lower raw storage-medium cost ($7/kWh for salt alone vs. Li-ion cells at ~$80–100/kWh). The low ~40% round-trip efficiency and the small-scale BOP cost penalty both erode the "cheap storage medium" advantage.

**The key first-principles insight**: molten-salt TES cost splits into a cheap, energy-scaling part (salt + tank volume, ~$/kWh) and an expensive, power-scaling part (pumps, heaters, HX, controls, ~$/kW) that's largely duration-independent. Li-ion cost scales almost linearly with kWh regardless of duration. So the crossover is governed by **storage duration at fixed power**, not absolute size: double the hours of storage at the same power rating, and TES's $/kWh roughly halves (cheap salt/tank increment) while Li-ion's doesn't move. This is why real deployments of molten-salt/thermal batteries (Malta, Rondo, Antora, etc.) target **long-duration (8h+) or multi-day** storage niches rather than the 2–4 hour daily-cycling market where Li-ion dominates — which is exactly the regime this 5 MWh / short-duration example falls into.
